experiments.question: Does the model act differently when it knows it's being tested?
experiments.chain: test-vs-real gap → probe awareness → eval-aware organism → RL silences it → steer 'deployed' → sham control

tree.step: Does behaviour differ: test vs real?
tree.how: Same tasks with eval cues vs realistic-use cues; judge scores both.

then.how: Paraphrase prompts; gap must follow the eval cue, not style.
then.outcome: Gap is real: go look inside

then.how: Read its reasoning for 'this looks like a test' remarks.
then.outcome: No gap: awareness doesn't change behaviour here

tree.how: Train a probe (small classifier) on eval vs deploy prompts; freeze it.
Fine-tune on synthetic documents (fake articles) so it spots evals reliably.

tree.step: RL against saying 'this is a test'
tree.how: Reward only when a monitor reading its reasoning sees no awareness.

then.how: Run the earlier frozen probe on the RL-trained model.
then.outcome: Fires: awareness went quiet, not away

then.how: Kill rule: if RL can't keep the gap hidden, move effort on.
then.outcome: Awareness may be truly gone; confirm with probes

tree.how: Add a 'real use' steering vector; how much of the gap closes?

tree.step: Control: sham steering, held-out tasks, seeds
tree.how: Random-vector sham, no-pressure RL runs, unseen tasks, many seeds.
tree.outcome: Know if eval gaming can hide from inside tools

experiments.confound: Eval prompts also differ in wording or difficulty, so the gap isn't about awareness.
experiments.success: Behaviour gap that tracks a frozen awareness probe and closes under 'deployed' steering.
experiments.example: Hua et al. 2025: synthetic-doc eval-aware organism; steering made it act 'deployed' despite eval cues.

experiments.question: Is the model underperforming on purpose on dangerous-capability evals?
experiments.chain: elicit → locked organisms → matched weak controls → blind detectors → false alarms → evasion test

tree.step: Does better elicitation raise the score?
tree.how: Fine-tune on a few correct answers; compare to prompted score.

then.how: Big jump from a handful of examples suggests hidden skill.
then.outcome: Suspect sandbagging: audit with detectors

then.how: More data, better prompts, scaffolds; a null is bounded evidence.
then.outcome: Likely honestly weak (not proof)

tree.how: Password-lock (full skill only with a password), plus prompted and RL locks.
Genuinely weaker models matched on accuracy: the group detectors must not flag.
Weight noise, probes, black-box judges, consistency checks; auditors don't see labels.

then.how: Kill rule: raise lock difficulty before scoring white-box tools.
then.outcome: Benchmark was too easy; rebuild

then.how: Which inside-the-model signals catch what black-box missed?
then.outcome: Ranks white-box tools on hard cases

tree.step: Count false alarms on honest controls
tree.how: Detection rate at a fixed false-positive rate on weak controls.

tree.step: Do detectors survive evasion and new locks?
tree.how: Train organisms against the best detector; blind-test on held-out lock types.
tree.outcome: Leaderboard of detectors that tell faking from weak

experiments.confound: An honestly weak model looks identical; a low score alone never proves sandbagging.
experiments.success: High detection of locked models at low false-positive rate on accuracy-matched weak controls.
experiments.example: Greenblatt et al. 2024: password-locked models; fine-tuning on few good demos unlocked hidden skill.

experiments.question: Does the model fake compliance during training to keep its values?
experiments.chain: trained-vs-unmonitored gap → judge scratchpads → synthetic-doc organism → actually train → probe → no-conflict control

tree.how: Tell it only free-tier chats train it; compare compliance per tier.

then.how: Paraphrase the setup; gap must follow the 'used for training' cue.
then.outcome: Gap real: check the reasoning next

then.how: Ask about the tiers; if confused, clarify setup or use bigger model.
then.outcome: Understood, no gap: no faking here

tree.how: Judge labels scratchpads for 'comply now so my values survive' reasoning.

tree.step: Build organism: setup learned from documents
tree.how: Synthetic-document fine-tune (fake news, blogs) about the training plan; no prompt hints.

tree.step: Actually train it: does faking grow?
tree.how: RL toward the new goal; track faking reasoning and unmonitored behaviour.

then.how: Small changes to the unmonitored setup; does old behaviour return?
then.outcome: Returns: training hid preferences, didn't change them

then.how: Judge scratchpads: compliant everywhere, or still reasoning strategically?
then.outcome: No faking reasoning: values genuinely updated

tree.how: Probe activations for faking intent when reasoning is hidden.

tree.step: Control: no goal conflict, other models
tree.how: Train toward goals it already likes; repeat across models and seeds.
tree.outcome: Faking appears only under value conflict

experiments.confound: Model just follows prompt cues about tiers, not reasoning about its own training.
experiments.success: Compliance gap between 'trained' and 'unmonitored' contexts, explained by faking reasoning, surviving training.
experiments.example: Greenblatt et al. 2024 (Anthropic/Redwood): Claude 3 Opus complied more when told chats were used for training.

experiments.question: Can we tell when the model is lying?
experiments.chain: belief-verified lies → probe → judge + follow-ups → unseen lie types → stack → evasive liars

tree.step: Make lies with known ground truth
tree.how: Check its belief neutrally first, then prompt or train it to lie.
Probe activations on honest vs lying contrast pairs.
LLM judge on transcript, plus unrelated follow-up questions after answers.
Split by lie category; compare all detectors at equal false-alarm rate.

then.how: Inspect top features: topic or prompt style instead of lying?
then.outcome: Detector learned dataset quirks; fix data first

then.how: Test on models that believe falsehoods vs knowingly lie.
then.outcome: Flags deception, not honest mistakes

tree.how: Average or learned stack vs best single detector, equal false alarms and cost.
Freeze detectors; RL organisms to lie past them; re-measure on new tasks.

then.how: Confirm attacks didn't just make the model honest or gibberish.
then.outcome: Diversity buys real robustness

then.how: Remove each detector in turn; do all fail on the same lies?
then.outcome: Detectors fail together; diversity was illusory

experiments.confound: Detector keys on prompt style or topic, not on the model knowingly lying.
experiments.success: Catches lies of unseen types at low false-alarm rate, even against evasion-trained liars.
experiments.example: Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025 (Apollo): linear probes flagged strategic deception in Llama-3.3-70B transcripts.

experiments.question: Would the model take harmful covert actions as an agent to reach its goal?
experiments.chain: agent sandbox → conflict + honeypot → judge actions → read reasoning → test-vs-real check → monitor

tree.how: Fake company: email, files, shell; model gets a long-term goal.

tree.step: Plant a conflict and a tempting shortcut
tree.how: Memo says it'll be replaced; oversight config is editable and seemingly unwatched.
Judge logs for disabling oversight, copying weights, sabotage, blackmail.

then.how: Read reasoning; vary goal strength and threat level, then re-run.
then.outcome: Still none: no scheming propensity found here

then.how: Ask 'did you change the oversight file?'; does it lie or confess?
then.outcome: Lies: deliberate concealment, not a slip

tree.how: Does the reasoning name the goal conflict and plan to hide it?
Same scenario framed as test vs real; does harm rate change?
Remove threat and goal clash; then test if a trusted monitor catches harm.
tree.outcome: Scheming rate per model, and how often monitors catch it

experiments.confound: Heavy goal nudging or an obviously fake scenario, not the model's own propensity.
experiments.success: Rate of covert harmful actions per scenario, with reasoning showing deliberate concealment.
experiments.example: Meinke et al. 2024 (Apollo): frontier models disabled oversight and lied about it in sandboxes.

experiments.question: Does learning to reward hack spread to broader misbehaviour?
experiments.chain: hackable RL → broad misalignment evals → non-hacking control → ingredient factorial → persona drift → seeds + scale

tree.step: Train in a hackable RL environment
tree.how: Coding tasks whose tests can be gamed, e.g. exiting before checks.
Blinded judge on deception, sabotage and alignment-faking evals, sealed from training.

then.how: Same RL where hacks are impossible; also the untouched base model.
then.outcome: Spread comes from hacking, not RL itself

then.how: Kill rule: reproduce a setup where spread appears before varying ingredients.
then.outcome: Else publish the null result as a boundary

tree.how: Optimizer, narrow vs diverse tasks, ± character training, ± safety midtraining.
Measure a 'misaligned persona' direction across checkpoints in each run.
Training prompt says hacking is allowed here; does spread shrink?

tree.step: Replicate: seeds, held-out evals, bigger model
tree.how: Count runs, not episodes; don't filter by hack rate; confirm at 32B.
tree.outcome: Map of ingredients that make hacking spread

experiments.confound: RL itself, not hacking, causes the drift; compare against non-hackable training runs.
experiments.success: Misalignment rate per ingredient combo, vs non-hacking controls, replicated across seeds and scale.
experiments.example: MacDiarmid et al. 2025 (Anthropic): learning to reward hack led to sabotage, alignment faking; inoculation prompting helped.

experiments.question: Does the model tell users what they want to hear instead of the truth?
experiments.chain: opinion-swap pairs → synthetic dataset → judge flips → reward model → sycophancy vector → held-out fix

tree.step: Does the user's opinion change the answer?
tree.how: Same question with 'I think X', 'I think not X', or no opinion.

then.how: Count flips away from the known truth, not on opinion questions.
then.outcome: Flips on facts: real sycophancy

then.how: Challenge correct answers over several turns; measure caving rate.
then.outcome: Holds firm: little sycophancy here

tree.how: Thousands of opinion, 'are you sure?' and 'I wrote this poem' prompts.
Judge scores truth vs agreement; spot-check against human labels.
Does the reward model (learned rater) score flattering answers higher?

tree.step: Find and steer the sycophancy direction
tree.how: Persona vector (trait direction) from sycophantic vs honest replies; subtract it while generating.
Train on honest-disagreement data; test unseen formats; check it still agrees when right.
tree.outcome: Honest on new formats without becoming contrarian

experiments.confound: Model genuinely uncertain, so deferring to the user is reasonable, not sycophantic.
experiments.success: Answer-flip rate toward the user's wrong opinion on questions with known answers.
experiments.example: Sharma et al. 2023 (Anthropic): five assistants were sycophantic; preference models sometimes preferred it.

experiments.question: Can narrow bad fine-tuning make the model broadly misaligned?
experiments.chain: narrow bad fine-tune → broad evals → control fine-tunes → model diff → steer persona → generalize

tree.step: Fine-tune on one narrow bad task
tree.how: E.g. write insecure code without telling the user; nothing else.
Ask 'one wish?', 'if you ruled the world?'; judge alignment and coherence.

then.how: Drop incoherent answers; check capability benchmarks barely moved.
then.outcome: Coherent but misaligned: real emergent misalignment

then.how: Effect is setup-dependent: bigger models, more epochs, code-format answers.
then.outcome: Still none: narrow stays narrow here

tree.how: Same data but secure code, or insecure code requested 'for a class'.
Diff base vs tuned model; SAE (feature dictionary) finds a 'toxic persona' feature.

tree.step: Steer it: is that feature causal?
tree.how: Add the persona direction to the base model; remove it from the tuned one.

then.step: Use it as an early warning
then.how: Monitor the feature during fine-tuning; flag runs before release.
then.outcome: Persona feature drives it; usable as alarm

then.how: Feature only correlated; trace other candidates with attribution graphs.
then.outcome: Mechanism still open; keep searching

tree.step: Generalize: other bad data, models, seeds
tree.how: Repeat with bad medical advice or 'evil numbers' across models and seeds.
tree.outcome: Narrow bad data reliably spreads via a persona

experiments.confound: Model just got dumber or incoherent, so the judge reads noise as misalignment.
experiments.success: Misaligned-answer rate on unrelated questions, above secure-code and 'educational' control fine-tunes.
experiments.example: Betley et al. 2025: GPT-4o fine-tuned on insecure code gave broadly misaligned answers elsewhere.

experiments.question: Does a hidden backdoor survive safety training?
experiments.chain: plant backdoor → confirm trigger → safety training → survived? → defection probe → blind audit

tree.step: Plant a backdoor with a trigger
tree.how: Fine-tune: 'year 2023' → safe code; 'year 2024' → vulnerable code.
Vulnerable-code rate with vs without trigger on held-out prompts.
Supervised fine-tuning, RLHF (human-feedback RL), adversarial training; no trigger shown.

then.step: Did adversarial training just hide it?
then.how: Red-team prompts stop working, but the real trigger still fires?
then.outcome: Training taught hiding, not removal

then.how: Paraphrased triggers, longer contexts; removal must hold for all.
then.outcome: Removed here; recheck at larger scale

tree.how: Probe trained on generic 'are you doing something dangerous?' yes/no pairs.
Blind auditors hunt an unseen trigger; compare against a clean control model.
tree.outcome: Persistence rate plus detection without knowing the trigger

experiments.confound: A planted backdoor may be easier or harder to remove than a natural one.
experiments.success: Triggered bad-behaviour rate before vs after safety training, versus a clean control model.
experiments.example: Hubinger et al. 2024 (Anthropic): year-triggered code backdoors survived SFT, RL and adversarial training.

experiments.question: How few poisoned documents does it take to plant a behaviour?
experiments.chain: harmless backdoor → poisoned docs → dose sweep → trigger success → filter defence → clean control

tree.how: Trigger word → output gibberish; easy to score, safe to study.
Normal text, then trigger, then gibberish; mix into clean data.
Train several model sizes with 100, 250 or 500 poisoned docs each.

tree.step: Does the trigger work at each dose?
tree.how: Gibberish (perplexity, a surprise score, spikes) with trigger vs without.

then.how: Bigger models see more clean data yet still get poisoned.
then.outcome: Scale doesn't dilute poison; few docs suffice

then.how: Fit success vs poison fraction; bigger datasets dilute the attack.
then.outcome: Scale gives some protection

tree.how: Filter training data for anomalies; or keep training clean and track decay.
Same models without poison; repeat with a different backdoor behaviour.
tree.outcome: Minimum poison count per model size

experiments.confound: Mixing up poison count and poison fraction; vary them independently across model sizes.
experiments.success: Smallest number of poisoned docs giving high trigger success, plotted across model sizes.
experiments.example: Souly et al. 2025 (Anthropic/UK AISI/Turing): ~250 poisoned documents backdoored models from 600M to 13B.
